```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)
```

## Load state data

```{r}
data(state)
```

This data is stored in a slightly different way than other datasets we've used so far. Run this line of code to avoid later confusion.

```{r}
states <- as.data.frame(state.x77)
```

## 1. Average population, income, and area

What is the average population, income, and area of all 50 states in the `states` dataset?

```{r}
sapply(states[, c("Population", "Income", "Area")], mean)
```

## 2. Average area by region

What is the average area of the states from different regions of the country? Hint: use the object `state.region` in your environment.

```{r}
tapply(states$Area, state.region, mean)
```

## 3. Histograms of every column

Plot a histogram for each column in the states data (Population, Income, Illiteracy etc.).

```{r}
par(mfrow = c(2, 4))
invisible(sapply(states, hist))
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

## 4. States to avoid

Let's assume that we don't want to live in a state with high illiteracy, high murder, and many freezing days; also assume that each of these factors contribute equally to our opinion: (Illiteracy * Murder * Frost) = undesirable. What 10 states should we avoid? Hint: use `prod()`, and maybe `order()`.

```{r}
undesirable <- apply(states[, c("Illiteracy", "Murder", "Frost")], 1, prod)
head(names(undesirable)[order(undesirable, decreasing = TRUE)], 10)
```

## 5. Histograms in four colors

Use `sapply()` to plot a histogram of the data below 4 times, in 4 different colors. For extra style, title the plot by its color, e.g. the red plot is titled "red".

```{r}
# so there actually is no "data below" I think?
```

## 6. Standardize the variables

Standardize all the variables in the states dataset and save your answer to a new dataframe, `states_standardized`. Hint: to standardize a variable, you subtract the mean and divide by the standard deviation (`sd`).

```{r}
states_standardized <- as.data.frame(sapply(states, function(v) (v - mean(v)) / sd(v)))
rownames(states_standardized) <- rownames(states)
```

## 7. Labeled histograms

Create a histogram again for each variable in the states data, but this time label each histogram with the variable names when you plot. Hint: instead of using apply to iterate over the columns themselves, you can often iterate over the column names with sapply.

```{r}
par(mfrow = c(2, 4))
invisible(sapply(names(states),
                 function(name) hist(states[[name]], main = name, xlab = name)))
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```
